extracted.intended_audience: general readers; students and scholars of ethics, philosophy, economics, and communication
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic article defining and illustrating the concept of mutual deceit, its necessary conditions, historical references, and applications in theater, business, and markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — mutual deceit
rubrics_metrics.description: Mutual deceit is a situation wherein lying is both accepted and expected or that the parties mutually accept the deceit in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: 'Mutual deceit is a situation wherein lying is both accepted and expected or that the parties mutually accept the deceit in question.' Example given: poker strategies that rely on deception and bluffing to win.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutuality requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Mutuality is essential — if the participants do not know the rules or do not accept them, then it is not considered mutual deceit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises knowledge and acceptance by participants as a necessary condition; without shared understanding of the 'rules' the situation does not qualify as mutual deceit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissibility: when untruths are not deception
rubrics_metrics.description: Untruths are permissible because they do not constitute lies when the source of information knows that those who receive it understand that it is untrue; in that case, no deception occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains moral/ethical status: if both parties recognize the message as untrue, withholding truth does not amount to deception. This is used to distinguish mutual deceit from standard lying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application — theatrical/fictional roles
rubrics_metrics.description: An actor assuming a role demonstrates mutual deceit: the audience understands the actor is not what he claims to be, so the untruth is given because everyone understands the fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: actor playing Romeo in Romeo and Juliet. Shows how shared conventions in theater create an accepted fiction that is not considered deceptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application — business as collusion/double reality
rubrics_metrics.description: In business, mutual deceit is phrased as a form of collusion that constructs a double reality for those inside or participating in it; truthfulness does not have intrinsic value in this framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguished from 'dual morality' (where managers set aside personal values to focus on profits). In mutual deceit, untruths are permissible because the receivers understand them to be untrue; cited sources discuss ethical implications for marketplace behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application — spot exchange market behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Spot exchange markets have mutual deceit characteristics: participants understand and accept that sellers underreport their true willingness-to-accept while buyers do the same for their true willingness-to-pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that sometimes even if a buyer does not explicitly accept that the seller lies, he implicitly does so by entering or participating in the market. This frames strategic misreporting as an accepted market convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/philosophical antecedents
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of mutual deceit has ancient usage: Homer and Hesiod cited it (along with theft and adultery) regarding the Greek gods; Plato noted it in criticism of poets; Blaise Pascal described human life as founded upon mutual deception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides intellectual history linking the concept to classical literature and Pascal's moral observations: used to contextualize mutual deceit as an enduring social-philosophical theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marxist critique/application
rubrics_metrics.description: Karl Marx cited mutual deceit as an offshoot of every new product created within bourgeois society — when the economic system creates new needs, people accept sacrifices to satisfy ego, producing a form of mutual deceit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framing connects mutual deceit to critiques of capitalism and the power of money in shaping needs and social relations; used as an analytical angle rather than a definitional condition.
